topic: Pure Fourier Series: The Power of Symmetry

outline.topic: Pure Fourier Series: The Power of Symmetry

sections.title: The Hook: The Whistle-Bot's Pure Tones
sections.content: Introduce the concept of complex periodic signals by using a 'Whistle-Bot' character. Explain that while most sounds are messy, the Whistle-Bot only understands pure, smooth oscillations (Sines and Cosines). The goal is to recreate a jagged 'Square Wave' jump using only these smooth movements.
sections.example: Visualizing a Whistle-Bot moving up and down in a jerky square pattern, then overlaying smooth sine waves to show the approximation.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Full Fourier Recipe
sections.content: Briefly review the Standard Fourier Series formula. Explain that any periodic function f(x) is a 'stew' of a constant (a0), Cosines (an), and Sines (bn). Emphasize the concept of 'Orthogonality'—that sines and cosines are like independent building blocks that don't mix.
sections.example: An animation of a kitchen blender where 'Cosine Carrots' and 'Sine Spinneys' are tossed in to create a 'Function Soup'.

sections.title: The Symmetry Filter: Even and Odd Functions
sections.content: Introduce symmetry as a way to simplify the 'stew'. Define Even functions (f(x) = f(-x)) as mirror reflections across the Y-axis and Odd functions (f(x) = -f(-x)) as rotational symmetry. Explain that Cosine is the 'Even King' and Sine is the 'Odd Queen'.
sections.example: A 'Symmetry Cat' sitting on the Y-axis. If the cat looks at a mirror and sees itself exactly, it's Even (Cosine-like). If it sees itself upside down on the other side, it's Odd (Sine-like).

sections.title: Deriving the Pure Sine Series
sections.content: Explain that if a function is Odd, all 'Even' components (Cosines) must have coefficients of zero (an = 0). This results in a 'Pure Sine Series'. Show the simplified integral formula for bn, noting that we only need to integrate over half the period (0 to L) and multiply by 2.
sections.example: A visual 'mathematical sieve' where a jagged Odd Wave passes through, trapping all Cosine terms in the mesh and letting only Sine terms flow through to the final equation.

sections.title: Deriving the Pure Cosine Series
sections.content: Conversely, if the function is Even, all 'Odd' components (Sines) vanish (bn = 0). This creates a 'Pure Cosine Series'. Highlight that the constant term a0 (the average value) remains here because a constant is also an 'Even' function.
sections.example: A graph of a 'Tent Map' function (Even). Watch the Sine waves try to fit but fail due to symmetry, leaving only the 'flat' a0 and the 'peaky' Cosines to reconstruct the shape.

sections.title: Application: Building the Square Wave
sections.content: Step-by-step calculation of a Pure Sine Series for a Square Wave (an Odd function). Show how adding the 1st, 3rd, and 5th harmonics gradually transforms a smooth wave into a sharp square corner.
sections.example: An animation of the 'Square-Wave Robot' from Section 1. As we add more Sine terms (1/n terms), the robot's path becomes flatter on top and steeper at the edges, demonstrating the Gibbs Phenomenon at the corners.

sections.title: Summary: Efficiency through Geometry
sections.content: Wrap up by emphasizing that Pure Fourier Series aren't just 'shorter' math; they represent the inherent physical symmetry of a system (like a vibrating string fixed at both ends).
sections.example: A split-screen view: One side shows a messy full equation, the other shows the elegant, 'Pure' version, highlighting the 50% reduction in computational effort.

storyboard.title: The Hook: The Whistle-Bot's Pure Tones
lecture_lines: Meet Whistle-Bot, a master of pure periodic tones.
Most sounds are messy, but Whistle-Bot prefers smooth oscillations.
He moves in a jerky, jagged square wave pattern.
Can we recreate this jump using only smooth movements?
Let's explore the power of mathematical symmetry.
animations: Whistle-Bot moves in a jerky square pattern (#FFD700).
A single smooth Sine wave appears (#ADD8E6).
Whistle-Bot's path is overlaid with the Sine wave.
Second harmonic Sine wave joins the sum (#90EE90).
Resulting wave starts looking like the square path.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Full Fourier Recipe
lecture_lines: Every periodic function is a mathematical "stew" of waves.
The recipe includes constants, cosines, and sine components.
These building blocks are independent and do not mix.
animations: Full Fourier formula appears in the center (#FFFFFF).
Highlight a0 in yellow (#FFFF00).
Highlight Cosine terms in blue (#0000FF).
Highlight Sine terms in green (#00FF00).
Icons for Sine and Cosine remain separate (Orthogonality).

storyboard.title: The Symmetry Filter: Even and Odd Functions
lecture_lines: Symmetry simplifies our mathematical "stew" significantly.
Even functions mirror perfectly across the vertical axis.
Odd functions exhibit rotational symmetry through the origin.
Cosines are the "Even Kings" of the wave world.
Sines serve as the "Odd Queens" in our series.
animations: Parabola y=x^2 mirrors across the Y-axis (#ADD8E6).
Cubic y=x^3 rotates 180 degrees through origin (#90EE90).
'Even King' Cosine graph flashes on the left (#ADD8E6).
'Odd Queen' Sine graph flashes on the right (#90EE90).

storyboard.title: Deriving the Pure Sine Series
lecture_lines: For odd functions, all cosine terms vanish to zero.
We are left with a pure sine series representation.
Integration only requires half the period, then double it.
animations: Odd Square Wave enters a 'Cosine Filter' box (#FFFFFF).
Cosine terms (an) are ejected from the filter (#FF0000).
an = 0 text appears in bold (#FF0000).
Formula for bn fades in with 2/L highlighted (#FFFF00).

storyboard.title: Deriving the Pure Cosine Series
lecture_lines: For even functions, all sine terms disappear completely.
This creates a pure cosine series for the function.
The constant average value, a0, remains an even component.
animations: Even Triangle Wave enters a 'Sine Filter' box (#FFFFFF).
Sine terms (bn) are ejected from the filter (#FF0000).
bn = 0 text appears in bold (#FF0000).
a0 (average value) stays with the Cosine terms (#FFFF00).

storyboard.title: Application: Building the Square Wave
lecture_lines: Let's build a square wave using our sine series.
Adding the first harmonic creates a basic smooth curve.
Higher odd harmonics sharpen the corners of the wave.
With enough terms, a jagged square shape emerges.
Watch the "ears" appear at the edges—the Gibbs Phenomenon.
animations: Plot y = sin(x) (fundamental frequency) (#ADD8E6).
Add y = 1/3 sin(3x) to the graph (#90EE90).
Add y = 1/5 sin(5x) to the graph (#FFFF00).
Highlight the 'ripples' near the jump (Gibbs Phenomenon).

storyboard.title: Summary: Efficiency through Geometry
lecture_lines: Pure series exploit the inherent symmetry of physical systems.
Symmetry reduces our computational work by half.
Elegant geometry makes complex math much more efficient.
animations: Left: Complex formula vs Right: Simple formula (#FFFFFF).
'50% Less Math' label appears on the right (#00FF00).
A vibrating string animation shows physical symmetry (#ADD8E6).
Closing text: 'Symmetry is efficiency' (#FFFFFF).
